claim: Thyroid hormone (TH) regulates diverse developmental events and can drive disparate cellular outcomes.
source: Thyroid hormone (TH) regulates diverse developmental events and can drive disparate cellular outcomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about TH function supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In zebrafish, TH has opposite effects on neural crest derived pigment cells of the adult stripe pattern, limiting melanophore population expansion, yet increasing yellow/orange xanthophore numbers.
source: In zebrafish, TH has opposite effects on neural crest derived pigment cells of the adult stripe pattern, limiting melanophore population expansion, yet increasing yellow/orange xanthophore numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript including cell counts and imaging, as well as citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: TH promotes maturation of both melanophores and xanthophores but in distinct ways.
source: We show that TH promotes maturation of both cell types but in distinct ways.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by transcriptomic analysis, cellular phenotyping, and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In melanophores, TH drives terminal differentiation, limiting final cell numbers.
source: In melanophores, TH drives terminal differentiation, limiting final cell numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data, melanin content measurements, binucleation analysis, and lysosomal content measurements presented in Figure 5 and related text.

claim: In xanthophores, TH promotes accumulation of orange carotenoids, making the cells visible.
source: In xanthophores, TH promotes accumulation of orange carotenoids, making the cells visible.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC analysis, gene expression data for carotenoid pathway genes, and scarb1 mutant analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: TH receptors act primarily to repress pigment cell maturation programs when TH is limiting.
source: TH receptors act primarily to repress these programs when TH is limiting.
evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue of pigment cell phenotypes in hypothyroid fish when TR genes are mutated, as shown in Figure 7.

claim: Fish lacking TH have about twice the normal number of melanophores and lack visible xanthophores.
source: fish lacking TH have about twice the normal number of melanophores and lack visible xanthophores (Figure 1A) (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 1A and citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing identified melanophores, xanthophores, iridophores, and multipotent pigment cell progenitors.
source: Dimensionality reduction (Becht et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2019) followed by unsupervised clustering identified melanophores, xanthophores and a third class of NC-derived pigment cells, iridescent iridophores (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the scRNA-seq analysis and UMAP visualization shown in Figure 2.

claim: A cluster likely corresponding to multipotent pigment cell progenitors was marked by genes encoding pigment cell transcription factors, general markers of mesenchymal NC and factors associated with proliferation and migration but not pigment synthesis.
source: A cluster likely corresponding to multipotent pigment cell progenitors (Budi et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2016) was marked by genes encoding pigment cell transcription factors, general markers of mesenchymal NC and factors associated with proliferation and migration but not pigment synthesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 2—Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations to prior work.

claim: Some cells within the progenitor cluster expressed the zebrafish-specific embryonic NC marker crestin.
source: Some cells within this cluster also expressed the zebrafish-specific embryonic NC marker crestin, which is generally down-regulated at later developmental stages but is still expressed in a subset of presumptive progenitor cells (Budi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to Budi et al., 2011.

claim: Euthyroid and hypothyroid trajectories were topologically equivalent.
source: Yet, euthyroid and hypothyroid trajectories were topologically equivalent.
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotemporal trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Pigment cell progenitors were not depleted in hypothyroid fish.
source: Moreover, pigment cell progenitors were not depleted in hypothyroid fish as might occur were these cells being allocated inappropriately as melanophores (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell type proportions shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hypothyroid fish exhibited a strong bias of pigment cell states towards earlier steps in pseudotime.
source: Yet, empirical distributions of pigment cell states in hypothyroid fish were all biased towards earlier steps in pseudotime, sometimes severely (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime distribution analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Genes expressed during terminal differentiation of melanophores from euthyroid fish (e.g. tfap2a, tyrp1b) were expressed at lower levels in melanophores of hypothyroid fish.
source: Genes expressed during terminal differentiation of melanophores from euthyroid fish (e.g. tfap2a, tyrp1b) were expressed at lower levels in melanophores of hypothyroid fish, suggesting an impediment to maturation in the absence of TH (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Melanophores of euthyroid fish tended to be uniformly well-melanized and stellate, whereas melanophores of hypothyroid fish were variably melanized and dendritic.
source: Melanophores of juvenile euthyroid fish tended to be uniformly well-melanized and stellate, whereas melanophores of juvenile hypothyroid fish were variably melanized and dendritic (Figure 5B), reminiscent of earlier stages of melanophore development in wild-type (Eom et al., 2012; Parichy and Turner, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 5B and citations to prior work.

claim: Melanophores of euthyroid fish are more heavily melanized than those of hypothyroid fish.
source: Quantification of melanin content within individual cells confirmed that melanophores of euthyroid fish are more heavily melanized than those of hypothyroid fish (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative melanin content measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Melanophores of euthyroid fish fail to divide whereas those of hypothyroid fish continue to do so.
source: Prior analyses indicated that melanophores of euthyroid fish fail to divide whereas those of hypothyroid fish continue to do so (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: Some stripe melanophores exhibited senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity when plated ex vivo.
source: When plated ex vivo, some stripe melanophores exhibited senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), although we were unable to score such staining reliably, precluding comparisons across TH conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lysosomal contents of melanophores from euthyroid fish were greater than melanophores from hypothyroid fish.
source: Lysosomal contents of melanophores from euthyroid fish were greater than melanophores from hypothyroid fish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Lysotracker fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Melanophores from juvenile euthyroid fish were larger than melanophores from hypothyroid fish.
source: Measurements of forward scatter (FSC-A) also suggested that melanophores from juvenile euthyroid fish were larger than melanophores from hypothyroid fish (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), although FSC-A can be influenced by cell-size-independent factors as well (Tzur et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, though the authors note caveats about FSC-A interpretation.

claim: In euthyroid fish, ~20% of melanophores were binucleate near the onset of adult melanophore differentiation but >50% were binucleate by juvenile stages.
source: In euthyroid fish, ~20% of melanophores were binucleate near the onset of adult melanophore differentiation but >50% were binucleate by juvenile stages, confirming an overall increase in binucleation with somatic stage and melanophore age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by binucleation quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ~70% of melanophores from euthyroid fish were binucleated, whereas only ~25% of melanophores from hypothyroid fish were in this state.
source: In stage-matched comparisons for TH status, ~70% of melanophores from euthyroid fish were binucleated, whereas only ~25% of melanophores from hypothyroid fish were in this state (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by binucleation quantification shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Most adult xanthophores develop directly from EL xanthophores that lose their pigment and then reacquire it late in adult pattern formation.
source: Most adult xanthophores develop directly from EL xanthophores that lose their pigment and then reacquire it late in adult pattern formation (Figure 3A) (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMenamin et al., 2014 and lineage diagram in Figure 3A.

claim: Fewer genes were expressed differentially between TH backgrounds in xanthophore than melanophore lineages (3.6% vs. 9%).
source: Indeed, fewer genes were expressed differentially between TH backgrounds in xanthophore than melanophore lineages (3.6% vs. 9%; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Several loci implicated in, or plausibly associated with, the processing of yellow/orange carotenoids were prominent among differentially expressed genes in xanthophores.
source: Prominent among these were several loci implicated in, or plausibly associated with, the processing of yellow/orange carotenoids (Figure 6B and C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), dietarily derived pigments that contribute to xanthophore coloration (Schartl et al., 2016; Toews et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6B and C, and citations to prior work on carotenoids.

claim: Carotenoids were detected by HPLC in skin containing xanthophores of euthyroid but not hypothyroid fish.
source: Differences in carotenoid gene expression suggested a corresponding pigmentation deficiency in xanthophores of hypothyroid fish that we confirmed by HPLC, histology, and transmission electron microscopy (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: scarb1 encodes a high-density lipoprotein receptor essential for carotenoid accumulation in birds and invertebrates.
source: Among carotenoid genes, scavenger receptor B1 (scarb1) encodes a high-density lipoprotein receptor essential for carotenoid accumulation in birds and invertebrates (Kiefer et al., 2002; Toomey et al., 2017) and we found it to be required in zebrafish for carotenoid deposition, although not cell persistence (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in other species and mutant analysis in zebrafish shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: scarb1 is required in zebrafish for carotenoid deposition, although not cell persistence.
source: Among carotenoid genes, scavenger receptor B1 (scarb1) encodes a high-density lipoprotein receptor essential for carotenoid accumulation in birds and invertebrates (Kiefer et al., 2002; Toomey et al., 2017) and we found it to be required in zebrafish for carotenoid deposition, although not cell persistence (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by scarb1 mutant analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: scarb1 was expressed more highly in xanthophores of euthyroid than hypothyroid fish.
source: scarb1 was expressed more highly in xanthophores of euthyroid than hypothyroid fish (q = 1.1E-10) (Figure 6B and E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and exogenous TH was sufficient to rescue both expression and carotenoid deposition (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6B, E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exogenous TH was sufficient to rescue both scarb1 expression and carotenoid deposition in hypothyroid fish.
source: scarb1 was expressed more highly in xanthophores of euthyroid than hypothyroid fish (q = 1.1E-10) (Figure 6B and E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and exogenous TH was sufficient to rescue both expression and carotenoid deposition (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TH treatment experiments shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In contrast to the defect of adult xanthophore pigmentation in scarb1 mutants, 5 dpf larval xanthophores were indistinguishable from wild-type.
source: In contrast to the defect of adult xanthophore pigmentation in scarb1 mutants, we found that 5 dpf larval xanthophores were indistinguishable from wild-type (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and analysis of larval xanthophores shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Mutants lacking xanthophore pigmentation at 5 dpf have normal adult xanthophores.
source: Conversely, mutants lacking xanthophore pigmentation at 5 dpf have normal adult xanthophores (Lister, 2019; Odenthal et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Carotenoids were undetectable in euthyroid 5 dpf larvae.
source: Carotenoids were undetectable in euthyroid 5 dpf larvae, and carotenoid-related genes were expressed at lower levels in EL xanthophores than adult xanthophores (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Carotenoid-related genes were expressed at lower levels in EL xanthophores than adult xanthophores.
source: Carotenoids were undetectable in euthyroid 5 dpf larvae, and carotenoid-related genes were expressed at lower levels in EL xanthophores than adult xanthophores (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression signature score analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Pteridine pathway genes tended to be expressed similarly across stages regardless of TH status and were even moderately upregulated in hypothyroid xanthophores.
source: By contrast, pteridine pathway genes tended to be expressed similarly across stages regardless of TH status and were even moderately upregulated in hypothyroid xanthophores (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression signature score analysis shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Pteridine autofluorescence and pterinosomes were indistinguishable between euthyroid and hypothyroid fish.
source: Pteridine autofluorescence and pterinosomes were also indistinguishable between euthyroid and hypothyroid fish (Figure 6—figure supplement 4D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2B) despite the overt difference in xanthophore color with TH status (Figure 1A; McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Genes encoding each of the three zebrafish TRs (thraa, thrab, thrb) were expressed by melanophores and xanthophores.
source: Genes encoding each of the three zebrafish TRs (thraa, thrab, thrb) were expressed by melanophores and xanthophores, yet presumptive null alleles for each unexpectedly had pigment cell complements and patterns that resembled the wild type (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Presumptive null alleles for each TR unexpectedly had pigment cell complements and patterns that resembled the wild type.
source: Genes encoding each of the three zebrafish TRs (thraa, thrab, thrb) were expressed by melanophores and xanthophores, yet presumptive null alleles for each unexpectedly had pigment cell complements and patterns that resembled the wild type (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging of TR mutants shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of thrab, on its own or in conjunction with loss of thraa, partially restored the deposition of carotenoids in interstripe xanthophores in hypothyroid fish.
source: Loss of thrab, on its own or in conjunction with loss of thraa, partially restored the deposition of carotenoids in interstripe xanthophoes; mutation of all three receptors fully rescued the number of carotenoid-containing xanthophores (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7B and C, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Mutation of all three TR receptors fully rescued the number of carotenoid-containing xanthophores in hypothyroid fish.
source: Loss of thrab, on its own or in conjunction with loss of thraa, partially restored the deposition of carotenoids in interstripe xanthophoes; mutation of all three receptors fully rescued the number of carotenoid-containing xanthophores (Figure 7B and C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: TR receptor mutations reduced the total numbers of melanophores in hypothyroid fish to levels indistinguishable from euthyroid fish.
source: TR receptor mutations likewise reduced the total numbers of melanophores in hypothyroid fish to levels indistinguishable from euthyroid fish (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by melanophore quantification shown in Figure 7D.

claim: There was no evidence for early pigmentation of xanthophores in euthyroid fish homozygous for thrab mutation.
source: Yet, we found no evidence for early pigmentation of xanthophores in euthyroid fish homozygous for thrab mutation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G), suggesting essential roles for other factors present only at later stages (Patterson and Parichy, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental timing analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TH normally curtails expansion of the adult melanophore population by ensuring that cells cease to divide in a timely manner.
source: We suggest a model in which TH normally curtails expansion of the adult melanophore population by ensuring that cells cease to divide in a timely manner; in hypothyroid fish, the inappropriate retention of an immature state allows continued growth of the melanophore population during these post-embryonic stages.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on integration of multiple lines of evidence including gene expression, cellular phenotypes, and proliferation data.

claim: In hypothyroid fish, the inappropriate retention of an immature state allows continued growth of the melanophore population during post-embryonic stages.
source: We suggest a model in which TH normally curtails expansion of the adult melanophore population by ensuring that cells cease to divide in a timely manner; in hypothyroid fish, the inappropriate retention of an immature state allows continued growth of the melanophore population during these post-embryonic stages.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on integration of multiple lines of evidence including gene expression, cellular phenotypes, and proliferation data.

claim: TH mediates a transition from pteridine-dependent pigmentation at embryonic/early larval stages to carotenoid-dependent pigmentation of the same cells in the adult.
source: These observations suggest that TH mediates a transition from pteridine-dependent pigmentation at embryonic/early larval stages to carotenoid-dependent pigmentation of the same cells in the adult.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on integration of gene expression data, HPLC analysis, and mutant phenotypes across developmental stages.

claim: Unliganded TRs normally repress maturation of melanophore and xanthophore lineages.
source: TR mutants lacked overt pigmentation defects yet allowed for rescues of both melanophore and xanthophore defects in hypothyroid fish, suggesting that unliganded TRs normally repress maturation of these lineages.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the rescue of pigment cell phenotypes in hypothyroid fish when TR genes are mutated.

claim: Loss of TRs allows the survival of congenitally hypothyroid mice.
source: Loss of TRs similarly allows the survival of congenitally hypothyroid mice (Flamant et al., 2002; Flamant and Samarut, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in mice.

claim: TRs may prevent the inappropriate activation of gene expression programs required for lineage maturation when TH levels are low.
source: TRs may therefore prevent the inappropriate activation of gene expression programs required for lineage maturation when TH levels are low, as is thought to occur during amphibian metamorphosis (Choi et al., 2015; Shi, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the data and comparison to amphibian metamorphosis.

claim: Stromal cells of the hypodermis and iridophores regulate melanophore and xanthophore numbers during adult pigment pattern formation.
source: Indeed, stromal cells of the hypodermis (Lang et al., 2009) and also iridophores (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013; Patterson and Parichy, 2013) regulate melanophore and xanthophore numbers during adult pigment pattern formation, and we observed striking differences in iridophore maturation depending on TH status.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and observations in the current study.

claim: Striking differences in iridophore maturation were observed depending on TH status.
source: Indeed, stromal cells of the hypodermis (Lang et al., 2009) and also iridophores (Frohnhöfer et al., 2013; Patterson and Parichy, 2013) regulate melanophore and xanthophore numbers during adult pigment pattern formation, and we observed striking differences in iridophore maturation depending on TH status.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in the scRNA-seq data and pseudotime analysis.

claim: Multipotent progenitors that give rise to adult melanophores, some xanthophores, and iridophores are established in the embryo and reside within peripheral nerves as development progresses.
source: Multipotent progenitors that give rise to adult melanophores, some xanthophores, and iridophores are established in the embryo and reside within peripheral nerves as development progresses (Budi et al., 2011; Budi et al., 2008; Camargo-Sosa et al., 2019; Dooley et al., 2013a; Singh et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on pigment cell lineages.

claim: The peripheral-nerve association of pigment cell progenitors in zebrafish is reminiscent of nerve-associated Schwann cell precursors that contribute to melanocytes of mammals and birds.
source: The peripheral-nerve association of pigment cell progenitors in zebrafish is reminiscent of nerve-associated Schwann cell precursors that contribute to melanocytes of mammals and birds (Adameyko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by citation to prior work in other species.

claim: Corresponding populations of embryonic and adult populations had largely overlapping transcriptomic states.
source: That corresponding populations of embryonic and adult populations had largely overlapping transcriptomic states additionally highlights the intriguing problem of how specific pathways are deployed reiteratively across life cycle phases to achieve specific morphogenetic outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined analysis of EL and adult cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Human melanoma is associated with hypothyroidism and recurrent TH pathway mutations.
source: Our findings are broadly consistent with a role for TH in balancing proliferation and differentiation (Brent, 2012) and may be of clinical relevance, as human melanoma is associated with hypothyroidism and recurrent TH pathway mutations (Ellerhorst et al., 2003; Shah et al., 2006; Sisley et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Melanoblasts derived from peripheral-nerve associated progenitors are proliferative during adult pigment pattern formation yet this activity largely ceases as the cells differentiate.
source: Melanoblasts derived from peripheral-nerve associated progenitors are proliferative during adult pigment pattern formation yet this activity largely ceases as the cells differentiate (Budi et al., 2011; McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the presence of TH, melanophores were more heavily melanized, larger, had greater lysosomal contents, and were more likely to be binucleated.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that TH promotes melanophore maturation to a terminally differentiated state: in the presence of TH, melanophores were more heavily melanized, larger, had greater lysosomal contents, and were more likely to be binucleated.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in Figure 5 and related supplements.

claim: TH promotes the melanization of melanoblasts ex vivo.
source: TH similarly promotes the melanization of melanoblasts ex vivo and a cessation of proliferative activity in vivo (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: TH promotes a cessation of melanophore proliferative activity in vivo.
source: TH similarly promotes the melanization of melanoblasts ex vivo and a cessation of proliferative activity in vivo (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: The yellow-orange color of xanthophores can depend on pteridine pigments, carotenoid pigments, or both.
source: The yellow-orange color of xanthophores can depend on pteridine pigments, carotenoid pigments, or both (Bagnara and Matsumoto, 2006; Granneman et al., 2017; Lister, 2019; Odenthal et al., 1996; Ziegler, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on xanthophore pigmentation.

claim: TH directly or indirectly regulates carotenoid-associated genes and carotenoid deposition.
source: We showed that TH directly or indirectly regulates carotenoid-associated genes and carotenoid deposition, allowing cryptic xanthophores to reacquire visible pigmentation.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating gene expression data, HPLC analysis, and mutant phenotypes presented in Figure 6.

claim: TH did not influence pteridine pathway genes.
source: TH did not similarly influence pteridine pathway genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression signature score analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cryptic xanthophores appear poised to re-differentiate.
source: In xanthophores at post-embryonic stages, then, TH drives a state of terminal differentiation from a developmental program that is relatively more advanced than that of progenitor-derived melanophores. That cryptic xanthophores appear poised to re-differentiate likely explains the smaller proportion of genes that were TH-dependent in these cells as compared to melanophores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of fewer TH-dependent genes in xanthophores compared to melanophores.

claim: The smaller proportion of genes that were TH-dependent in xanthophores as compared to melanophores is explained by cryptic xanthophores being poised to re-differentiate.
source: In xanthophores at post-embryonic stages, then, TH drives a state of terminal differentiation from a developmental program that is relatively more advanced than that of progenitor-derived melanophores. That cryptic xanthophores appear poised to re-differentiate likely explains the smaller proportion of genes that were TH-dependent in these cells as compared to melanophores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of fewer TH-dependent genes in xanthophores compared to melanophores and their developmental history.

claim: Cells of subcluster melanophore 2 exhibited low levels of transcriptional activity and expressed fewer genes, suggesting a more advanced state of differentiation, as compared to cells of melanophore 1.
source: For example, cells of subcluster melanophore 2 exhibited low levels of transcriptional activity and expressed fewer genes, suggesting a more advanced state of differentiation, as compared to cells of melanophore 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of UMI counts and gene expression shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells of xanthophore 1 had fewer transcripts and expressed fewer genes than cells of xanthophore 2, suggesting they may represent undifferentiated, cryptic xanthophores and actively differentiating populations, respectively.
source: Likewise cells of xanthophore 1 had fewer transcripts and expressed fewer genes than cells of xanthophore 2, suggesting they may represent undifferentiated, cryptic xanthophores and actively differentiating populations, respectively (McMenamin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of UMI counts and gene expression, and citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: Reduced total RNA content is associated with a G0 cell state (i.e. quiescence, replicative senescence, and/or terminal differentiation).
source: Reduced total RNA content is associated with a G0 cell state (i.e. quiescence, replicative senescence, and/or terminal differentiation) (Coller et al., 2006; Darzynkiewicz et al., 1980); low median UMI counts in sub-clusters of melanophores and xanthophores (mel 2, xan 1) suggest alternative states within these differentiated cell populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on RNA content and cell state.

claim: Low median UMI counts in sub-clusters of melanophores and xanthophores (mel 2, xan 1) suggest alternative states within these differentiated cell populations.
source: Reduced total RNA content is associated with a G0 cell state (i.e. quiescence, replicative senescence, and/or terminal differentiation) (Coller et al., 2006; Darzynkiewicz et al., 1980); low median UMI counts in sub-clusters of melanophores and xanthophores (mel 2, xan 1) suggest alternative states within these differentiated cell populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on UMI count analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and knowledge about RNA content and cell state.

claim: Cell clusters with lower median UMIs (mel 2, xan 1) exhibited gene expression trends indicative of curtailed transcriptional and translational activity.
source: However, cell clusters with lower median UMIs (mel 2, xan 1) exhibited gene expression trends indicative of curtailed transcriptional and translational activity, including reduced expression of AP-1 transcriptional complex members (AP1 TF signature score), and genes involved in unfolded protein response (UPR signature score), and proliferation (cell-cycle signature score) (Chinenov and Kerppola, 2001; Maurus et al., 2017; Patil and Walter, 2001; Riabowol et al., 1992) (for details of genes in signature scores, see Supplementary file 2—Table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression signature score analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citations to prior work.

claim: Melanophores and xanthophores in subclusters with lower total UMI counts (mel 2, xan 1) expressed fewer unique genes compared to cells in the other subcluster regardless of equivalent UMI counts.
source: Melanophores and xanthophores in subclusters with lower total UMI counts (mel 2, xan 1) expressed fewer unique genes compared to cells in the other subcluster regardless of equivalent UMI counts, consistent with a more restricted gene expression profile of these populations (shaded areas indicate standard error bounds).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: More genes were expressed at higher levels in xanthophore 2 compared to xanthophore 1, and in melanophore 1 compared to melanophore 2.
source: These analyses revealed more genes, expressed at higher levels in xanthophore 2 compared to xanthophore 1, and in melanophore 1 compared to melanophore 2. These biases were consistent with xanthophore 2 and melanophore 1 representing more active cells, and xanthophore 1 and melanophore 2 representing less active cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Melanophore and xanthophore subclusters were differentially distributed along trajectory branches.
source: Melanophore and xanthophore subclusters were differentially distributed along trajectory branches in Figure 3D, consistent with xanthophore 2 and melanophore 2 representing cells at later steps of maturation as compared to xanthophore 1 and melanophore 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Transcripts per cell declined in melanophores but not iridophores during maturation.
source: For example, transcripts per cell declined in melanophores but not iridophores, consistent with an expectation of reduced RNA abundance as melanophores—but not iridophores—exit the cell cycle with maturation (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B) (Budi et al., 2011; Darzynkiewicz et al., 1980; McMenamin et al., 2014; Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of UMI counts over pseudotime shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and citations to prior work.

claim: The expression score for cell-cycle genes was greater for iridophores than melanophores at the terminal step of pseudotime.
source: The expression score for cell-cycle genes was greater for iridophores than melanophores at the terminal step of pseudotime (p<0.0002; Wilcoxon; pseudotime bin 8; n = 91 iridophores, 319 melanophores), consistent with iridophores continuing to proliferate even after differentiation, and melanophores normally failing to do so (Budi et al., 2011; Darzynkiewicz et al., 1980; McMenamin et al., 2014; Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell-cycle signature scores shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and citations to prior work.

claim: Iridophores continue to proliferate even after differentiation, and melanophores normally fail to do so.
source: The expression score for cell-cycle genes was greater for iridophores than melanophores at the terminal step of pseudotime (p<0.0002; Wilcoxon; pseudotime bin 8; n = 91 iridophores, 319 melanophores), consistent with iridophores continuing to proliferate even after differentiation, and melanophores normally failing to do so (Budi et al., 2011; Darzynkiewicz et al., 1980; McMenamin et al., 2014; Spiewak et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with cell-cycle gene expression data.

claim: Addition of exogenous TH to hypothyroid cells ex vivo can promote differentiation of unpigmented melanoblasts to melanophores.
source: Indeed, prior analyses showed that addition of exogenous TH to hypothyroid cells ex vivo can promote differentiation of unpigmented melanoblasts to melanophores (McMenamin et al., 2014), contrary to the idea that TH specifically blocks melanophore development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McMenamin et al., 2014.

claim: Euthyroid melanophores contained more melanin than those of hypothyroid fish.
source: Melanophores of euthyroid fish contained more melanin than those of hypothyroid fish (F1,2710=271.2, p<0.0001), after controlling for individual variation among fish within TH conditions (F10,2710=8.5, p<0.0001; sample sizes: n = 1180 cells from five euthyroid fish, n = 1542 cells from five hypothyroid fish).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of melanin content measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: If planar areas of concentrated melanin granules are assumed spherical, then euthyroid melanophores had on average ~1.7 x the total melanin content of hypothyroid melanophores.
source: If planar areas of concentrated melanin granules are assumed spherical, then euthyroid melanophores had on average ~1.7 x the total melanin content of hypothyroid melanophores.
evidence: This is a calculation based on melanin area measurements.

claim: Fully differentiated melanophores of zebrafish are often binucleate.
source: Fully differentiated melanophores of zebrafish are often binucleate (Usui et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usui et al., 2018.

claim: Euthyroid fish had proportionally more binucleate melanophores than hypothyroid fish.
source: Euthyroid fish had proportionally more binucleate melanophores than hypothyroid fish (χ2=230.3, d.f. = 1, p<0.0001) after controlling for a higher incidence of binucleation in developmentally more advanced fish overall (11.5–13 SSL; χ2 = 5.5, d.f. = 1, p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of binucleation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Dorsal and ventral stripe melanophores did not differ significantly in binucleation frequency.
source: Individual points indicate proportions of binucleate melanophores observed in dorsal stripes (circles) and ventral stripes (diamonds), which did not differ significantly (p=0.8; sample sizes: n = 383 melanophores in four euthyroid fish, n = 706 melanophores in three hypothyroid fish).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of binucleation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Xanthophores plated ex vivo did not exhibit SA-β-gal staining.
source: Xanthophores plated ex vivo did not exhibit SA-β-gal staining.
evidence: This claim is supported by SA-β-gal staining experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lysotracker dye did not stain melanosomes despite some similarities between melanosomes and lysosomes.
source: Lysosomes were revealed in tyrp1b:palm-mCherry+ (magenta) melanophores by Lysotracker dye (cyan), which did not stain melanosomes (yellow) despite some similarities between these organelles (Raposo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Raposo et al., 2007.

claim: Melanosomes and lysosomes have some similarities.
source: Lysosomes were revealed in tyrp1b:palm-mCherry+ (magenta) melanophores by Lysotracker dye (cyan), which did not stain melanosomes (yellow) despite some similarities between these organelles (Raposo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Raposo et al., 2007.

claim: Lysosomal content revealed significantly greater normalized mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of Lysotracker dye in melanophores from euthyroid fish as compared to hypothyroid fish.
source: Lysosomal content revealed significantly greater normalized mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) of Lysotracker dye in melanophores from euthyroid fish as compared to hypothyroid fish (euthyroid, 20,423 melanophores from 10 fish; hypothyroid, 87,252 melanophores from 10 fish; p<0.01, Wilcoxon).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of Lysotracker fluorescence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FSC-A values were higher for euthyroid compared to hypothyroid cells overall.
source: FSC-A values were higher for euthyroid compared to hypothyroid cells overall [p<0.001; cells are the same as in (C) ], consistent with an overall difference in cell size.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Euthyroid fish at a later stage of pattern formation exhibited a higher proportion of binucleate melanophores compared to those at earlier stages.
source: Euthyroid fish at a later stage of pattern formation exhibited a higher proportion of binucleate melanophores compared to those at earlier stages (early, 7.2 SSL: n = 153 in five fish; late, 11 SSL: n = 477 melanophores in five fish; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of binucleation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SA-β-gal staining results from lysosomal β-gal activity.
source: SA-β-gal staining results from lysosomal β-gal activity and both β-gal activity and lysosome number increase in aging cells (Kurz et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on SA-β-gal and lysosomes.

claim: Both β-gal activity and lysosome number increase in aging cells.
source: SA-β-gal staining results from lysosomal β-gal activity and both β-gal activity and lysosome number increase in aging cells (Kurz et al., 2000; Lee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on cellular aging.

claim: Human nevus melanocytes and melanophores of teleost melanoma models exhibit senescent or senescent-like phenotypes and can be multinucleated.
source: Human nevus melanocytes, and melanophores of teleost melanoma models, exhibit senescent or senescent-like phenotypes and can be multinucleated (Leikam et al., 2015; Leikam et al., 2008; Regneri et al., 2019; Savchenko, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on melanocyte senescence and multinucleation.

claim: Multinucleation is a condition linked to increased cell survival and size.
source: Finally we examined multinucleation, a condition linked to increased cell survival and size (Orr-Weaver, 2015; Usui et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on multinucleation.

claim: Carotenoid pathway gene expression score was higher in xanthophore lineage cells of euthyroid fish compared to hypothyroid fish.
source: Carotenoid pathway gene expression score was higher in xanthophore lineage cells of euthyroid fish compared to hypothyroid fish (p=1.5E-15, Wilcoxon).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression signature scores shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Pteridine pathway gene expression was marginally lower in xanthophore lineage cells from euthyroid fish compared to hypothyroid fish.
source: By contrast, pteridine pathway gene expression was marginally lower in cells from euthyroid fish (p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression signature scores shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Carotenoids are normally localized to lipid droplets.
source: Carotenoid pigments are normally localized to lipid droplets, the presence of which can be revealed by Oil-red-O staining.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carotenoid localization.

claim: A proportion of aox5:palmEGFP+ xanthophores stained ex vivo from euthyroid fish contained lipid, whereas xanthophores from hypothyroid fish were never observed to have such lipid contents.
source: Here, a proportion of aox5:palmEGFP+ xanthophores stained ex vivo from euthyroid fish (n = 112 cells) contained lipid (red), whereas xanthophores from hypothyroid fish (n = 48 cells) were never observed to have such lipid contents.
evidence: This claim is supported by Oil-red-O staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ultrastructurally, carotenoids and lipids are detectable as electron-dense carotenoid vesicles.
source: Ultrastructurally, carotenoids and lipids are detectable as electron-dense carotenoid vesicles (red circles) (Djurdjevič et al., 2015; Granneman et al., 2017; Obika, 1993), which were observed in xanthophores from euthyroid but not hypothyroid fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and citations to prior work.

claim: Electron-dense carotenoid vesicles were observed in xanthophores from euthyroid but not hypothyroid fish.
source: Ultrastructurally, carotenoids and lipids are detectable as electron-dense carotenoid vesicles (red circles) (Djurdjevič et al., 2015; Granneman et al., 2017; Obika, 1993), which were observed in xanthophores from euthyroid but not hypothyroid fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Zebrafish scarb1 mutants had a 105 bp, in-frame deletion in a conserved region of the protein.
source: Zebrafish scarb1 mutants had a 105 bp, in-frame deletion in a conserved region of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: scarb1 mutants lacked mature, interstripe xanthophores but had normal stripes and aox5:palmEGFP expression, suggesting that patterning and unpigmented xanthophores were normal.
source: scarb1 mutants lacked mature, interstripe xanthophores but had normal stripes and aox5:palmEGFP expression, suggesting that patterning and unpigmented xanthophores were normal.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In hypothyroid fish treated with exogenous TH (T4), scarb1 expression was rescued within ~1 d and carotenoid autofluorescence of xanthophores was recovered within ~2 d.
source: In hypothyroid fish treated with exogenous TH (T4), scarb1 expression was rescued within ~1 d (upper) and carotenoid autofluorescence of xanthophores was recovered within ~2 d (lower).
evidence: This claim is supported by TH treatment experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: At 5 dpf, scarb1 mutants had yellow larval xanthophores with wild-type levels of pteridines.
source: At 5 dpf, scarb1 mutants had yellow larval xanthophores with wild-type levels of pteridines.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Carotenoids were not detectable in EL zebrafish (5 dpf, wild-type).
source: Carotenoids were not detectable in EL zebrafish (5 dpf, wild-type; compare to Figure 3D); csf1ra mutants, which lack xanthophores, had HPLC profiles indistinguishable from wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: csf1ra mutants, which lack xanthophores, had HPLC profiles indistinguishable from wild-type at 5 dpf.
source: Carotenoids were not detectable in EL zebrafish (5 dpf, wild-type; compare to Figure 3D); csf1ra mutants, which lack xanthophores, had HPLC profiles indistinguishable from wild-type.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Pteridine signatures between EL, hypothyroid, and euthyroid xanthophores were more similar than carotenoid signatures.
source: Pteridine signatures between EL, hypothyroid, and euthyroid xanthophores were more similar than carotenoid signatures.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression signature score analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Ammonia-induced pteridine fluorescence was present in adult xanthophores of both euthyroid and hypothyroid fish.
source: Ammonia-induced pteridine fluorescence was present in adult xanthophores of both euthyroid and hypothyroid fish (red arrowheads).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Numbers of visible xanthophores and melanophores were not distinguishable between euthyroid fish wild-type or homozygous mutant for TR mutations either singly or in combination.
source: Numbers of visible xanthophores and melanophores were not distinguishable between euthyroid fish wild-type or homozygous mutant for TR mutations either singly or in combination (p>0.1) and are shown combined here.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of cell counts shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Homozygous thrab mutation partially rescued numbers of pigmented xanthophores in hypothyroid fish.
source: Homozygous thrab mutation partially rescued numbers of pigmented xanthophores and more fully rescued numbers of melanophores in hypothyroid fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Homozygous thrab mutation more fully rescued numbers of melanophores in hypothyroid fish.
source: Homozygous thrab mutation partially rescued numbers of pigmented xanthophores and more fully rescued numbers of melanophores in hypothyroid fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Somatic mutagenesis of thraa in fish homozygous mutant for thrab mutants (thrab thraa*) did not significantly enhance the rescue of xanthophore maturation or melanophore numbers.
source: Somatic mutagenesis of thraa in fish homozygous mutant for thrab mutants (thrab thraa*) did not significantly enhance the rescue of xanthophore maturation or melanophore numbers.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: Somatic mutagenesis of thrb in fish doubly homozygous mutant for thraa and thrab (thrab thraa thrb*) rescued xanthophore maturation to wild-type levels in the absence of TH.
source: By contrast somatic mutagenesis of thrb in fish doubly homozygous mutant for thraa and thrab (thrab thraa thrb*) rescued xanthophore maturation to wild-type levels in the absence of TH.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Carotenoids persisted in hypothyroid fish mutant for thrab.
source: HPLC revealed persisting carotenoids in hypothyroid fish mutant for thrab (boxed region), in contrast to the absence of detectable carotenoids in hypothyroid fish that were wild-type for thrab (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Stage of first xanthophore appearance did not differ significantly between euthyroid fish that were heterozygous or homozygous wild-type for thrab mutation.
source: Stage of first xanthophore appearance did not differ significantly (p=0.7) between euthyroid fish that were heterozygous or homozygous wild-type for thrab mutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1G.

claim: TH coordinates post-embryonic development of NC and other derivatives through mechanisms that are incompletely characterized.
source: Thyroid hormone (TH) coordinates post-embryonic development of NC and other derivatives through mechanisms that are incompletely characterized (Brent, 2012; Brown and Cai, 2007; Sachs and Buchholz, 2017; Shi, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on TH and development.

claim: During the abrupt metamorphosis of amphibians, TH drives outcomes as disparate as tail resorption and limb outgrowth.
source: During the abrupt metamorphosis of amphibians, TH drives outcomes as disparate as tail resorption and limb outgrowth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TH function in amphibian metamorphosis.

claim: The more protracted post-embryonic development of zebrafish has similarities to fetal and neonatal development of mammals.
source: In the more protracted post-embryonic development of zebrafish—which has similarities to fetal and neonatal development of mammals (Parichy et al., 2009)—TH coordinates modifications to several traits including pigmentation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Parichy et al., 2009.

claim: In zebrafish post-embryonic development, TH coordinates modifications to several traits including pigmentation.
source: In the more protracted post-embryonic development of zebrafish—which has similarities to fetal and neonatal development of mammals (Parichy et al., 2009)—TH coordinates modifications to several traits including pigmentation.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the data presented in the manuscript and prior work.

claim: Mechanisms that synchronize developmental signals and integrate them across cell types and organ systems remain poorly defined but are fundamentally important to both development and evolution of adult form.
source: Mechanisms that synchronize developmental signals and integrate them across cell types and organ systems remain poorly defined but are fundamentally important to both development and evolution of adult form (Atchley and Hall, 1991; Ebisuya and Briscoe, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on developmental coordination.

claim: NC cells disperse throughout the body, contributing peripheral neurons and glia, osteoblasts and chondrocytes, pigment cells and other derivatives.
source: NC cells disperse throughout the body, contributing peripheral neurons and glia, osteoblasts and chondrocytes, pigment cells and other derivatives.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural crest cell derivatives.

claim: Differences in the patterning of NC-derived cells underlie much of vertebrate diversification.
source: Differences in the patterning of these cells underlie much of vertebrate diversification.
evidence: This is a general statement about the evolutionary importance of neural crest cells, supported by established knowledge.

claim: The neural crest is a key innovation of vertebrates.
source: A powerful system for elucidating how organisms coordinate fate specification and differentiation with morphogenesis is the array of cell types that arise from embryonic neural crest (NC), a key innovation of vertebrates (Gans and Northcutt, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gans and Northcutt, 1983.
